rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient that spans the full solvent-strength range at a moderate temperature to reveal the overall elution window and whether any compounds are strongly retained. The 20 min slope is a balanced first pass that should show both early crowding and late elution behavior without being excessively shallow.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only improvement is reducing t_last below 10 min. Keep the same solvent window and temperature and make the gradient steeper to compress the chromatogram while checking whether the current critical pair near rows 6–7 remains above R = 1.5.

The 14 min gradient achieved the time target but over-compressed the critical 6–7 pair, while 20 min had ample resolution. Try the intermediate slope at the same window and temperature to recover that pair toward R >= 1.5 while keeping t_last under 10 min.

We need a small gain in retention selectivity for the critical 6–7 pair without pushing the last peak much later than 10.5 min. Lowering temperature one step at the same gradient should slightly expand separations, letting us see whether improved resolution outweighs any modest increase in t_last.

Temperature changes hurt selectivity, so return to 40 C and instead narrow the gradient window slightly at the same fast slope. Lowering phi1 should reduce overall solvent strength enough to spread the mid-gradient cluster around peaks 5–7 while likely keeping the last peak near or under 10 min.

Compared with the 0.95 window, lowering phi1 improved the critical 6–7 pair while still keeping t_last below 10 min at 14 min gradient time. A small increase to 16 min should push that pair to full resolution, and with the narrower window there is a good chance t_last stays close enough to 10 min for a higher overall CRF.

At constant tG = 14 min, reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical 6–7 pair with only a modest increase in t_last, so push one more step to 0.85. This should further spread the mid-cluster while likely keeping the last peak close enough to 10 min to improve on the current best.

At phi1 = 0.85 and tG = 14 min all pairs are resolved, so the next step is to steepen the gradient and try to pull t_last back under 10 min. This checks whether the extra selectivity gained from the narrower window is enough to keep the 6–7 pair acceptable even at a shorter gradient time.

The narrower window at 12 min lost too much resolution on the critical 6–7 pair, while 0.90/14 was the current best. Testing 0.90/12 maps the time–selectivity tradeoff at the shorter gradient and helps confirm whether 14 min is already near optimal or if there is still room to gain speed.

The limiting issue remains the dense mid-cluster, not the late peak, so shift the whole gradient slightly stronger at the start while keeping the successful 0.90/14/40 framework. Raising phi0 may selectively compress the early region and alter spacing within peaks 5–7 enough to improve the critical pair without a large penalty in t_last.

Raising phi0 to 0.10 improved both t_last and the critical 6–7 pair at 14 min, so now combine that benefit with the narrower upper-end window that previously increased mid-cluster resolution. This is a targeted attempt to push the 6–7 pair to full credit while keeping the last peak near 10 min.

You have reached the maximum score, so the only useful remaining test is to find the shortest method before resolution drops below full credit. Shorten tG by one step at the same composition window and temperature to see whether the perfect method can be made faster while preserving all pairs at R >= 1.5.

Since shortening tG lost the critical 6–7 pair, keep the proven composition program and probe whether a small temperature increase can pull t_last just under 10 min while retaining full resolution. This tests if the perfect method has a slightly faster equivalent at higher temperature.

The 0.10/0.85/14/40 method is already perfect, but t_last sits just above 10. Testing a slightly lower phi1 at the same tG and temperature probes whether the mid-cluster can stay fully resolved while shifting selectivity enough to keep or improve the score around the optimum.

Increasing phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved both speed and the critical 6–7 separation, so test one more step higher while keeping the proven phi1, tG, and temperature. This is a focused check for a still faster fully resolved method around the current optimum.

This is now a better perfect method than the previous one because it keeps full resolution with a shorter t_last, so the next optimization step is to shorten tG. Testing 12 min at the same phi0/phi1 and temperature checks whether this faster starting composition preserves the critical 6–7 pair at full resolution.

Increasing phi0 from 0.10 to 0.15 preserved perfect resolution and further reduced t_last, so test one more step higher at the same phi1, tG, and temperature. This explores whether an even stronger start still keeps the critical 6–7 pair above 1.5 while giving the shortest perfect method found so far.

Phi0 = 0.20 was too strong and hurt the critical 6–7 pair, so keep the successful phi0 = 0.15 and test a slightly lower phi1 to see whether that restores or improves selectivity while remaining in the short, fully resolved region. This is the most plausible nearby composition change for another perfect method with comparable or better speed.

The local optimum appears centered at phi0 = 0.15, and lowering phi1 to 0.80 increased resolution but pushed t_last above 10 min. Testing the opposite side at phi1 = 0.90 maps the remaining neighborhood and could reveal an equally perfect but slightly faster method than the current best.

The composition neighborhood around 0.15/0.85/14 is best, and temperature has only been tested away from this phi0. A 5 C decrease may slightly increase retention and possibly improve the already marginal 6–7 selectivity, testing whether this same composition can remain perfect while clarifying temperature sensitivity near the optimum.

Use one remaining run to bracket temperature effects at the original perfect composition, since both 35 C and 45 C degraded selectivity and may indicate a narrow optimum or nonmonotonic behavior. Testing 25 C determines whether much lower temperature restores the favorable spacing or confirms that 40 C is uniquely best.

With the maximum CRF already achieved, use a remaining run to confirm the local time–resolution tradeoff around the best composition by checking the one-step longer gradient. This should show whether the critical 6–7 pair has extra margin at essentially the same selectivity center, reinforcing that 14 min is the shortest perfect method in this neighborhood.

With only a few runs left and the optimum already found, map the last unexplored side of the upper-end composition at the best phi0 and tG. This checks whether a stronger final solvent can preserve full resolution while giving an even shorter fully resolved method, though the current trend suggests the critical 6–7 pair may tighten.

Use a remaining run to probe the lower-phi1 side at the faster 12 min gradient, where current data suggest a balance between stronger selectivity and short run time. This helps complete the local map around the optimum and checks whether any 12 min method can unexpectedly recover full credit on the critical pair.

For the final run, test the one remaining nearby 12 min combination most likely to recover full resolution: the higher phi0 that improved speed and the lower phi1 that improved the critical 6–7 separation. This is the best last chance to find a shorter perfect method than the current 14 min optimum.
